opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the key insight for us was that a relational database is really a graph in disguise. If you think about it, every row in every table is an entity — a customer, a product, a transaction — and the primary key–foreign key relationships between tables are essentially edges connecting those entities. So instead of doing what people traditionally do, which is to manually join tables together and hand-engineer features into one big flat table, we take the database as it is and turn it into what we call a relational entity graph. Each row becomes a node, the node's attributes are the column values in that row, and the foreign key links become edges.

And the nice thing is that this graph is heterogeneous — you have different node types for different tables, different edge types for different relationships — and it's also temporal, because a lot of rows have timestamps. Transactions happen at specific times, users sign up at specific times. So you have to respect time very carefully: when you make a prediction at a given moment, the model should only see the part of the graph that existed up to that point, otherwise you leak information from the future.

Once you have that representation, you can apply graph neural networks directly. The GNN does message passing along those primary–foreign key links, so information flows from, say, a customer's transactions to the products they bought, to other customers who bought those products, and so on. What that effectively means is the neural network learns the joins and aggregations itself — the kinds of things a data scientist would otherwise spend weeks writing SQL for. Each column gets encoded according to its type, numerical, categorical, text, timestamp, into an embedding, and then the GNN learns how to combine all of that across tables.

That's the core idea behind what we've called relational deep learning: treat the database natively as a graph, learn end-to-end over it, and skip the manual feature-engineering pipeline. And what we've seen is that this matches or beats expert-built feature pipelines while taking a tiny fraction of the human effort.

r001.rationale: It says each row in every table becomes a node in the relational entity graph.

r002.rationale: It describes primary key–foreign key links between rows as edges connecting the corresponding entities.

r003.rationale: It proposes applying a GNN directly to the graph and says predictions should use only the graph available at the prediction time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've been thinking about for a long time, and I think the key insight is actually pretty simple once you see it. A relational database is, at its heart, already a graph. People just don't usually think of it that way.

So think about what a database looks like. You have a set of tables. Each table has rows, and each row is an entity: a customer, a product, a transaction, a doctor visit, whatever the domain is. And then you have these primary key and foreign key relationships that link rows in one table to rows in another table. A transaction row points to a customer row and points to a product row. That is literally an edge in a graph. The foreign key is the edge.

So what we do is we take the database and we say, every row becomes a node, every foreign key becomes an edge, and the node type is the table the row came from. What you end up with is what we call a relational entity graph. It's a heterogeneous graph, meaning you have different types of nodes and different types of edges, and the schema of the database becomes the schema of the graph. And the nice thing is this is lossless. You haven't flattened anything, you haven't thrown anything away. The multi-table structure is still fully there, it's just now in a form that a neural network can consume.

And then there's a second piece, which is what do you do with the columns. Each row has attributes, and those attributes come in different modalities. Some are numerical, some are categorical, some are timestamps, some are free text, maybe even images. So you need per-column encoders that take each of these raw values and map them into an embedding, and then you combine those column embeddings into an initial representation for the node. This is kind of the tabular deep learning piece of the problem. In our open-source work we have a library called PyTorch Frame that handles exactly this, and then PyTorch Geometric handles the graph part.

Once you have that, you can run a graph neural network on top. The GNN does message passing: a node looks at its neighbors, which are the rows it's linked to through foreign keys, aggregates their representations, updates itself, and you repeat that for a few layers. So after two or three layers, the embedding of a customer node has effectively summarized that customer's transactions, the products in those transactions, maybe the categories of those products, and so on. And this is exactly what a data scientist would be doing by hand with feature engineering, writing joins and aggregations, except here it's learned end to end from the data and from the prediction task.

The one thing you have to be really careful about is time. Databases are not static, rows get added over time, and if you're not careful the model sees the future when it's making a prediction about the past. So every row carries a timestamp, and when you build the computation graph for a prediction at a given point in time, you only let it see rows that existed before that time. That temporal consistency is honestly where most of the engineering subtlety lives, and it's what makes the whole thing honest as a predictive system rather than a leaky one.

So the short version is: rows are nodes, foreign keys are edges, columns get encoded into node features, and a GNN learns over that structure while respecting time. We call this whole approach relational deep learning, and I think it's a very natural way to get neural networks to work directly on the data that most enterprises actually have, which is sitting in these multi-table databases, not in nicely curated single tables.

r001.rationale: It says every database row becomes a node, with each row representing an entity.

r002.rationale: It says foreign keys become edges linking the corresponding rows in different tables.

r003.rationale: It proposes running a GNN over the graph and learning from the data for a prediction task.

astra-6.text:
The natural way to think about a relational database is as a graph. Each row in a table becomes a node, and foreign-key relationships become edges between those nodes. The columns in a row give us the attributes of that node. And because we have different tables, we have different types of nodes and different types of relationships.

For example, imagine you have customers, orders, and products. A customer connects to their orders, and each order connects to the products that were purchased. A graph neural network can then pass information along those connections, learning how to combine a customer’s attributes with information about their purchases and the products involved.

What’s powerful here is that we preserve the relational structure. Instead of manually joining everything into one big table and deciding ahead of time which aggregates to compute, we let the model learn which information to gather and how to combine it for a particular prediction task.

r001.rationale: It states that each row in a table becomes a node.

r002.rationale: It represents foreign-key relationships between rows as edges connecting their nodes.

r003.rationale: It proposes using a graph neural network to learn over those connections for a prediction task.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that a relational database already defines a graph. Every row in a table becomes a node, and the foreign-key relationships between rows become edges. The columns in each row give us the attributes of that node. And because you have different tables, you have different types of nodes and different types of relationships.

Then you can use a graph neural network to pass information along those relationships. For example, imagine you have customers, orders, and products. To make a prediction about a customer, the model can learn from that customer’s attributes, but also from their orders and the products in those orders. It learns how to combine that information for the prediction task, instead of requiring somebody to manually construct a big, flat table with all the relevant features.

So the key idea is to preserve the relational structure and let the neural network learn across it.

r001.rationale: It says every table row becomes a node.

r002.rationale: It says foreign-key relationships between rows become edges, connecting the related records.

r003.rationale: It proposes using a graph neural network to learn across the relational graph for a prediction task.
